title: One Byte Costs Cloudflare 250GB of Memory (title from repo catalog .prism/shared/pot/catalog_local.json; no description file present)
core_takeaway: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 resolver (a Rust service called Big Pineapple) holds ~250 billion DNS cache entries, so one wasted byte per entry costs ~250GB of RAM fleetwide. Five layout-level changes cut the per-entry footprint from 953 to 420 bytes (56%) and allocated memory from 1.1KB to 461 bytes (58%), freeing roughly 100TB of RAM while also making inserts 43% faster and lookups 19% faster. Every change came from looking at what the data actually does at runtime — cache entries are write-once, read-many — rather than from algorithmic cleverness.
key_points: Big Pineapple is Cloudflare's Rust DNS resolver behind 1.1.1.1, holding over 250 billion cache entries at any one time.

Change 1: entries were full of Vecs, but cache entries are written once and never grown, so the Vec's capacity field (a usize, 8 bytes) plus over-allocated spare heap was pure waste. Swapping Vec for Box (and String for boxed str) across eight fields saved 64 bytes per entry and over 15TB fleetwide.

Change 2: the answer, authority and additional record lists are always written together, read together and in the same order, so three lists (3 x pointer+length = 48 bytes, 3 heap allocations) became one list plus two u16 offsets (4 bytes), saving 28 bytes per entry plus struct-padding savings.

Change 3: every record stored its owner domain even though the query domain was already the cache key, so the field became an Option<Box<Name>> storing None when it matches — saving a whole heap allocation per record while still handling CNAME chains where the owner genuinely differs.

Change 4: the record-data enum was always as large as its biggest variant (NAPTR at 136 bytes, 144 with tag and padding), so an A record needing 4 bytes occupied 144. Boxing the big variants (TXT, SVCB, NAPTR) left A and AAAA inline and saved ~120 bytes each, which matters because the benchmark traffic mix is 56% A and 25% AAAA.

Boxing introduced two new costs: jemalloc rounds allocations up into fixed size bins (a 40-byte MX record lands in a 48-byte bin, quietly losing 8 bytes), and boxed data loses cache locality, forcing an extra cache-line fetch through a pointer.

Change 5 is the middle ground that undoes both costs: keep the rest of the entry structured, but store all record data as one boxed u8 array with each record written as a 2-byte length prefix plus its bytes — one allocation, contiguous, no per-record bin rounding.
Measured outcome: per-entry 953 to 420 bytes, allocated 1.1KB to 461 bytes, insert throughput 625K to 893K entries/sec (+43%), lookups 828ns to 670ns (19% faster).
In production, P99 resident memory fell from 9.3GB to 5.3GB (43%), roughly 100TB fleetwide, about 130 servers' worth of RAM, which will be reinvested as a larger cache.
why_it_matters: It is a clean worked example of profiling the shape of your data rather than your algorithms: every win came from noticing that stored values never grow, repeat the key, or sit in an enum sized for a rare variant. The Box-vs-Vec, merged-list-with-offsets and length-prefixed-bytes patterns transfer directly to any hot in-memory index or cache in a tooling suite, and the boxing regression is a reminder that allocator bin rounding and cache locality can eat a paper win. The closing framing — the 2018 design was right for 2018 economics — is a useful rule for when to revisit a data layout at all.

key_moments.label: Big Pineapple: the Rust resolver behind 1.1.1.1
Change 1: Vec capacity overhead on write-once entries
Change 2: three record lists merged into one plus offsets
Change 3: dropping the redundant owner name
The boxing trade-off: jemalloc bin rounding and lost locality
Change 5: store record data as length-prefixed raw wire bytes
Production impact: P99 memory 9.3GB to 5.3GB, ~100TB freed
Closing: was the original layout premature optimization?
